1.1: 1.1 Preface. In Hebrew, VAIICRA. ISICHIUS on Leviticus. This book is called Leviticus because the subject of the whole book is made plain in this name. The tribe of Levi received by lot the ministry of the tabernacle, in which it was commanded that sacrifices, firstfruits, and offerings of the firstborn be offered, since all sacrifices belong to the Levites (Num. 18). From them this book fittingly took its name, for it sets out all these things in order. In Latin it is called the Book of Offering, or of Sacrifice, because it treats of sacrifices and ceremonies. It is rightly placed after Exodus: for in Exodus the tabernacle is ordained, and in this book are contained the things that the Lord spoke to Moses about the tabernacle, and the ceremonies of the tabernacle. But if anyone asks why the books of the law are divided, when the history is undivided in time, the answer is: so that the division of the books may take away the weariness of the reader, just as a traveler divides the stages of the road, so that the labor, being divided, is lessened. Rabanus gathered much from Isichius, bishop of Jerusalem, who expounded Leviticus quite fully, and he added to his work certain things from other Fathers also who expounded some of his opinions, and out of the confused order of the opinions he composed a certain order of exposition by alternating the opinions of many doctors. ISICHIUS on Leviticus. Above all it is necessary to draw the interpretation of the law toward the anagogical sense, and to search out the spiritual understanding in the letter. For this does not contradict the law but defends it. That the spiritual understanding must be diligently sought, Christ himself also showed, who in his parables (Matt. 13) called the field the world; the farmer sowing good seed, the just; the weeds, the wicked; the reapers, the angels; and the enemy who sowed over it, the devil. Who then forbids us to call the ox the one who works justice; the sheep, the simple man; the dove, the innocent; and the turtledove, those who act on a higher plane and have leisure for contemplation? Did not Ezekiel call Jerusalem a lioness, and her cub Eliachim, who was led into Egypt, and another cub Joachim, led into Babylon (Ezek. 19)? Not only what is said in parables, but also what is said according to history, must be led to a higher understanding, as Paul shows, saying: It is written that Abraham had two sons, etc.; after which he added: Which things are said by way of allegory: for these are the two Testaments, etc. (Gal. 4). Perhaps, however, the letter stripped of spiritual understanding will be harmful, and liable to various reproaches. Hence through Ezekiel the Lord calls the law both good and not good, saying: I gave them my precepts, and showed them my judgments, which if a man do, he shall live in them. And elsewhere: I gave them precepts that were not good, and judgments in which they shall not live. It is plain therefore that there are good precepts and not good ones; and ones in which they live and ones in which they do not live: for he who keeps the Holy Spirit lives in them; but he who lives according to the flesh dies, because he does not find life in them. Then, the lawgiver wished the surface of the law to be kept not always, but for a fixed time, in order to restrain the hard neck of the Jews; hence: I know that this people is stiff-necked (Exod. 32); and Hosea calls the Jews a heifer that kicks in rebellion, that is, one that can in no way be tamed. And elsewhere: Ephraim is a heifer taught to love to tread out the grain, and I passed over the beauty of her neck (Hosea 10); in which obedience is signified. For he laid on the yoke of the law so that, humbled, they might willingly take up the light and sweet yoke of the Gospel (Matt. 12). ORIGEN, homily 1 on Leviticus. If, as some even of our own do, we follow the simple understanding, and without any twist of word, as they themselves are wont to laugh at us, and without the cloud of allegory, receive the voice of the lawgiver, then I, a churchman living under the faith of Christ and placed in the midst of the Church, am compelled by the authority of the divine precept to sacrifice calves or lambs, and to offer fine flour with frankincense and oil. Therefore the Lord himself, the Holy Spirit himself, must be entreated to deign to remove every cloud of sin that darkens the sight of our heart, so that we may behold the spiritual understanding, according to that: Open my eyes, and I will consider wondrous things, etc. (Ps. 118). ISIDORE. Every variety of victims prefigured the victim of Christ. Hence, when the truth was offered, the shadow ceased (1 Cor. 15), prefiguring the true sacrifice of the true and eternal priest. Now the reason that one true victim of Christ was promised by the victims of animals offered for cleansing was that in it there would be forgiveness of sins contracted from flesh and blood, which shall not possess the kingdom of God: for the bodily substance will be changed into a heavenly quality. Christ was offered in the calf on account of the power of the cross; in the lamb, on account of innocence; in the ram, on account of headship; in the goat, on account of the likeness of the flesh of sin; in the turtledove and the dove, because he is God and man. For the Mediator of God and men was shown in the union of two substances; in the mixing of the fine flour, it was shown that the Church, that is, the body of Christ, is gathered together by the water of baptism of those who believe. And we morally offer a calf when we overcome the pride of the flesh; a lamb, when we correct irrational impulses; a kid, when we overcome wantonness; a dove, while we are simple; a turtledove, while we are chaste, or while we preserve chastity; unleavened loaves, when we feast not on the leaven of malice, but on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. RABANUS. He says that each single sacrifice, indeed almost each single syllable, and the garments of Aaron, and the whole order of Leviticus breathe heavenly sacraments. Origen also says: Just as in the last days the Word of God came forth into the world clothed in flesh from the Virgin Mary, whose flesh was seen by all, while the divinity was veiled, known to a few and chosen ones: so the word of God is brought forth to men through the prophets, there covered with the veil of flesh, here with the veil of the letter. The letter is seen as the flesh; the spiritual sense is perceived as the divinity. He called, etc. ISICHIUS on Leviticus. By a conjunction he joins what follows to what precedes; that is, the beginning of this book with the end of the preceding: for the work of one and the same day is contained in both. The book of Numbers also, since it has nothing between itself and Leviticus, receives a similar opening; that is: And the Lord spoke to Moses in the desert of Sinai, etc. (Num. 1). So the people did nothing after the history of Leviticus before the history of Numbers: for they had not changed place, because they had not yet dedicated the tabernacle, nor had much time passed. For in the first month of the second year, at the beginning of the same month, they began to act. But in Exodus and Genesis, because much time had passed in between, from the death of Joseph and the departure of the children of Israel, the conjunction does not hold at the beginning, but a fitting opening is arranged for their dispensation: These are the names of the children of Israel who entered into Egypt. ISICHIUS. According to the Seventy: He called back. Just as according to them God called back Bezalel by name, when he commanded the tabernacle to be made according to the pattern which was shown on the mountain: so now too he commanded a certain image of intelligible sacrifices to be described; this calling back indeed hints at a certain dispensation of things or words looking toward higher things. ORIGEN, homily 1 on Leviticus. And he called, etc. In the beginning, etc., down to who bring clean inner ears to hear these things. ISICHIUS on Leviticus. That God does not love the sacrifices of the Jews, etc., down to and plainly this calling hints at a dispensation of words or things looking toward higher things. ORIGEN, homily 1 on Exodus. The man whom he first set to offer to the Lord, etc., down to the sacrifice also is twofold, because it saves both earthly and heavenly things. THE SAME, ibid. The man who, made in the image and likeness of God, lives rationally, etc., down to and his neck like that of a turtledove. ISICHIUS on Leviticus. He designates the simple man, etc., down to salvation is granted even to beasts of burden. THE SAME. God demands sacrifice so that it may profit us, not himself, etc., down to who at last may bear witness for us or against us.
1.3: 1.3 Of the herd, etc. ISIDORE. The first sacrifice is the calf, that is, Christ, born of the herd, that is, of the stock of the patriarchs, who with the plow of his cross tamed the land of our flesh, and enriched it with the seed of the Holy Spirit, with the fruit of virtues. ORIGEN, as above. The proud calf is our flesh, etc., down to but they did not have the oil of charity and peace and the other virtues. To make the Lord favorable, etc. According to the Seventy, however, he says this is acceptable to the one offering; that is, if it is truly acceptable to us, and our heart judging rightly and clinging to no passion has approved the gift as worthy to be received: then we can pray in the sight of the Lord, that is, obtain forgiveness. Hence before him we shall persuade our hearts, because if our heart reprehend us, we know that God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things, etc.
1.4: 1.4 And he shall lay, etc. What we call a victim is called in Greek [holocaust], in which the intelligible holocaust is signified. For he bears fruit spiritually who by a spiritual manner of life is made a holocaust: for this reason the one who offers lays his hand upon the head of the victim, which signifies the beginning of the aforesaid manner of life, and the one who offers is himself the cause of his own promise. For he offers willingly, because it is a gift, and every gift is voluntary. For if he transgresses his promise, he accuses himself, when he has paid the penalty. Thus it will be acceptable, and will serve for his expiation, when by the laying on of the hand he has made manifest that he offered willingly and not of necessity.
1.5: 1.5 And he shall immolate, etc. ISICHIUS on Leviticus. For we owe to God not only our own conscience and manner of life, etc., down to as Christ is called the door, so is the apostolic teaching which he bestows. The sons of Aaron. ORIGEN, where above. Annas and Caiaphas were of the race of Aaron, and the others who pronounced Christ guilty of death, and poured out his blood at the base of the altar: for he was killed where the altar was and its base, whence: It cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem.
1.6: 1.6 And having flayed, etc. ORIGEN, ibid. The priest strips off the skin, etc., down to he joined earthly things with heavenly, and human things with divine. THE SAME. He commands the entrails with the feet to be washed with water, as a sign of baptism. He washes the entrails who purifies the conscience; he washes the feet who receives the consummation of the sacrament. For he that is clean needs not but to wash his feet, but is clean wholly (John 15): nor can anyone have part with Jesus unless he has washed his feet. ISICHIUS on Leviticus. The skin is stripped off when we are despoiled of riches and whatever worldly things, etc., down to imitating Christ as far as we can. GREGORY, book 1 of the Moralia, chap. 40. We strip the skin of the victim, etc., down to let him place nothing slippery on the altar of his prayer.
1.10: 1.10 But if, etc. ISICHIUS on Leviticus. With few changes he says the same things, etc., down to whence: The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, etc. A yearling, etc. ISIDORE. The lamb offered is the innocent Christ crucified. Hence: Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sins of the world. Rightly is a kid offered, because by the death of Christ the devil, the author of sin, is slain. ISICHIUS. This he did not command concerning oxen, etc., down to therefore it is called a holocaust even without the working of justice.
1.11: 1.11 At the side, that is, the altar looks toward the Gentile world, because the passion of Christ was celebrated for the nations. And we offer the sacrifice at the northern side of the altar, when we believe, remembering it, that the passion of Christ was undergone for the nations.
1.13: 1.13 He shall burn all. He commands the one offering to place all these things upon the altar so that we may fit our whole man to the spiritual Scriptures which are spoken of the intelligible altar of the Lord's body, and strive to live in imitation of him. And the odor. When our sacrifice becomes a holocaust, and we offer all things upon the intelligible altar, conforming the manner of our life to him as imitators of Christ, then a most sweet odor is offered to the Lord.
1.14: 1.14 But if, etc. ISIDORE. The turtledove is the flesh of Christ, according to that of Solomon: Thy cheeks are beautiful as the turtledove's. The dove signifies the Holy Spirit. Hence: He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending as a dove, this is my Son. The turtledove-and-dove therefore is the flesh of Christ joined to the Spirit: these three sacrifices man offers, that is, Christ, namely from oxen, from flocks, and from birds. ISICHIUS on Leviticus. Wonderful is the subtlety of the words, etc., down to they contemplate and savor heavenly things, where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God.
2.2: 2.2 A soul, etc. From the better part he signifies the whole man: for he requires a spiritual and perfect hearer, because it is the soul that is capable of wisdom, not the flesh. ISIDORE. A soul, etc. The fourth sacrifice the soul offers. The fine flour signifies the Church, which is gathered from many persons as from grains, ground by the mill of the law and the Gospel, divided between the letter and the spirit, united by the water of baptism, anointed with chrism, and made firm by the spiritual fire; through humility it becomes an acceptable victim. ORIGEN, homily 2 on Leviticus. A soul. Which has neither a calf, etc.; down to with the oil of divine mercy or grace. Mystically, it signifies, as in the place: All the souls that went into Egypt with Jacob, etc. (Gen. 46). And Luke says: And we were in the ship in all two hundred seventy-six souls (Acts 27). Perhaps by soul he signifies the Gentile. For above he commanded the children of Israel to offer sacrifices with blood. But here, commanding the one who is without the law to offer, he does not say man, as above, but soul. The Gentile was animal [natural], not understanding the things that are of God, but is called to the offering by the mercy of God, that he may receive salvation; when he arranges sacrifices for sins, he who has neither sheep nor goat is commanded to offer a turtledove or dove; and he who has not even that, fine flour. For he is no longer saved by works, as one poor in virtues, but by the knowledge of God alone, which, although it is the beginning of salvation, yet frankincense and oil are to be added, that grace may be mingled with alms and prayers. Hence the angel says to Cornelius: Thy prayers and thy alms are ascended to the Lord (Acts 10). In frankincense the inward passions are healed, and by its smoke eyes weeping from infirmity are cured. For the prayer of the soul heals the passions, cures the inner eyes of ignorance, and drives away the tears kindled by the sickness of sin. The sons, the ministers of the Church; because whatever we offer, we ought to confer with the holy doctors of the Church. Hence Paul conferred the Gospel with the apostles, lest he should run in vain (Gal. 2). Of whom. The unity of the Church takes a handful of fine flour, because each of the faithful ought to seek knowledge of the Scripture according to the capacity of his understanding. Hence: Not to be more wise than it behooveth to be wise, but to be wise unto sobriety. Of whom one, etc. (Rom. 12). It should be noted that a handful of the fine flour and of the oil is commanded to be offered, but all the frankincense; because the wisdom which is signified in the fine flour, and the charity or mercy which is signified in the oil, cannot be full in this life. Hence: We see now through a glass in a dark manner; and, Now I know in part, etc. (1 Cor. 12). A part of the oil too is offered, because mercy is never fulfilled, since even if you show mercy as much as you can, you ought still to wish to do more. Charity also, which is figured by the oil, is begun in the present, and will be perfected in the future. But the frankincense is wholly burned, because prayer is always to be persisted in. Of fine flour. Of the knowledge or understanding of God. For the knowledge that faith can grasp is acceptable to God, and just as he who wishes to grasp more with a handful profits nothing, for all runs through: so faith is the measure of the knowledge of God. For he that cometh to God must believe, and whatever is not of faith is sin (Heb. 11). A memorial, etc., the perfect knowledge of the understanding of God, which we shall remember, and which is never destroyed; and it destroys that which is now, not as contrary to it, but shows by its own fullness that it is the smallest part: For when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away (1 Cor. 13).
2.3: 2.3 Of the sacrifice, etc. ISICHIUS on Leviticus. Namely, of that perfect knowledge hidden in the heavens and laid up in Christ, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2). Aaron is interpreted 'mountain-dweller,' that is, understanding higher things about God; or 'secret,' as having in himself the law of God and the oracles: such a one can offer the sacrifice. The holy of holies is from the offerings to the Lord: for what remains is divided, yet surpassing all knowledge and exalting to perfection.
2.4: 2.4 When thou offerest a sacrifice, etc. ISICHIUS, ibid. The sacrifice is Christ immolated for us. Baked in the oven, that is, of the virgin, namely the womb. For an oven receives bread and fire: so the womb of the virgin received the bread of life, that is, the Word of God, and the fire of the Holy Spirit from heaven. Hence: The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, etc. (Luke 1). If then you offer the gift of the incarnation of Christ, which was accomplished in the womb of the virgin, it is not acceptable to God unless it is made of fine flour, that is, the knowledge or understanding of God. For on this matter we receive the discourse from the apostles and the prophets. The words of the apostles are loaves; those of the prophets, wafers. For as much as loaves are better suited to nourish than wafers, so much do the words of the apostles excel the words of the prophets. Both however are unleavened, without the leaven of worldly knowledge. Yet both are made with oil, for it was written by them in agreement about the mercy of Christ, because apostles and prophets wrote, but the apostles wrote more fully, who showed fulfilled what those announced as to come. Wafers. A broad and thin bread, which signifies prophecy and the law; for as much as lies between the solidity of bread and the thinness of a wafer, so much lies between the Gospel and the words of the law and the prophets: yet these are anointed with oil, because the law and prophecy foretold the charity of Christ, by which he came for the salvation of the human race.
2.5: 2.5 If thy oblation be, etc. ISICHIUS on Leviticus. The oblation from the frying pan, etc., down to and therefore he withdrew from his knowledge. Of fine flour mixed, etc. Because he died and had mercy on us. Without leaven, that is, without blemish.
2.6: 2.6 Thou shalt divide it into little pieces: so that we may divide the account of his sufferings, which came upon him in parts, and diligently distinguish the blows, that is the buffetings, the spittings, and the wounds. And thou shalt pour over it, etc., so that as he mercifully died for us, we too may show mercy to our brothers even to death. From the frying pan. For as the frying pan is midway between the fire and the food, so in a certain way the cross is midway between the impassible divinity and the humanity, which was roasted with the fire of the passion. And as in a frying pan soft things grow hard and hard things grow soft, so in the passion of the cross stony hearts were softened, and soft and flowing ones made firm. To offer a sacrifice from the frying pan, therefore, is to discuss the mystery of the cross with veneration.
2.7: 2.7 But if from, etc. ISICHIUS on Leviticus. As in the frying pan the cross, etc., down to for out of mercy he endured death and dispensed the resurrection. But if, etc. Morally, he offers fine flour who strives to conduct himself well in some of the ordinary uses of common life. This is to be sprinkled with oil, because every soul needs the oil of mercy, and cannot escape the present life unless heavenly mercy is at hand. The oven expresses the weight of temptation, the frying pan the constancy and strength of the mind, the gridiron manifold assault.
2.11: 2.11 Every oblation. ORIGEN, homily 2 on Leviticus. Let someone say, etc., down to in this way more truly and perfectly you offer sacrifices according to the Gospel, which Israel can no longer offer according to the law. Of leaven and honey. Nothing voluptuous, nothing sweet pleases God, but what has something of sharpness and severity. Hence the Passover is eaten with bitter herbs. And of honey. Of Gentile eloquence, which is sweet in voice, not in substance. Hence: The lips of a harlot are a dripping honeycomb (Prov. 5). But what is said in the Canticle: Honey and milk are under thy tongue (Cant. 4), does not contradict the present words. For it says under the tongue, not on the tongue, to show that the wisdom of the pagans and the letter of the Jews are subject to the tongue of the Church, that is, to its doctrine. Of these he does not wish the whole teaching to be offered. Hence he says: It shall not be burned for a sacrifice, that is, a holocaust: only their firstfruits you shall offer. For we offer the firstfruits of that wisdom, not the whole, as Paul says to the Athenians: As some also of your own poets said: For we are also his offspring. For what he found fitting to the knowledge of God, he did not reject: yet he did not multiply testimonies further, because it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe; hence Moses says: But upon the altar they shall not be laid, and although it might have been said, they shall not be placed, he says: They shall not be laid for a sweet savor: signifying that if we try to obtain knowledge of the divinity from external things, such a sacrifice does not ascend to the altar, but is pressed down among earthly things, because it is of the earth. BEDE on Leviticus, vol. 2. That honey was not offered in the sacrifice of God, etc., down to we pass over all imperfect things.
2.13: 2.13 Thou shalt season with salt, and shalt not take away the salt of the covenant. Apostolic wisdom. Hence: You are the salt of the earth, etc. (Matt. 5). As all food is seasoned with salt, so the apostolic teaching is the word of preaching. Therefore salt is commanded to be offered in every sacrifice, so that we may live according to the apostolic teaching and institution and the imitation of their work. Hence Paul says: Be ye followers of me, as I also am of Christ (1 Cor. 4). And elsewhere: Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Eph. 2). Hence the lawgiver also did not say simply salt, but, the salt of the covenant of thy God. For as the covenant is rational, so also is the salt rational. He wished therefore to remind us of the Gospel testament and the Apostolic salt. Oil is offered in sacrifice if we offer with cheerfulness, not out of sadness or of necessity. For God loveth a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9). Salt, which has an astringent power and is contrary to honey, is commanded to be added to the sacrifices: salt is a symbol of prudence, which restrains and dries up pleasure. In every oblation, etc. For that cannot please God which has not been corrected to the norm of his will. For if in human affairs one of the wise men of this world admonished that we must act with such caution as to say: Every action ought to be free of rashness and negligence: what must be thought concerning the things of God? But if thou offer, etc. ORIGEN, book 1 on Leviticus. In the second place, of the firstfruits, etc., down to because the letter was being separated from the spirit. ISICHIUS. Thou shalt break it in the manner, etc. He commanded them not only the knowledge of God, etc., down to for through alms and prayer divine knowledge is perfected in us.
3.1: 3.1 But if the victim, etc. ORIGEN, homily 3 on Leviticus. Passing over the rest, he speaks of the salutary sacrifices, which are offered from animals, that is, oxen and goats and sheep, and nothing further is substituted for immolation: not even the birds, which were substituted above in the offering of gifts. For he who offers salutary victims is conscious of his own salvation: he therefore has need to offer great and perfect things, hence the Apostle: But strong meat is for the perfect (Heb. 5). ISICHIUS. But if the victim, etc. There are according to the laws different manners of life among men, etc., down to for they ought to conduct themselves worthily, that they may come to salvation. Male or female, etc. ISICHIUS. Above only males are offered for the holocaust, etc., down to that is, weak works with stronger ones.
3.3: 3.3 The fat that, etc. THE SAME. It is fitting that the intelligible fat be offered, etc., down to and by deliberation let us sanctify the mass. The vitals. The Seventy: The belly, that is, the heart, of which he makes mention the second time according to the Seventy, because according to physicians it has a twofold operation: by one part it draws in nourishment, which they call the upper belly; by the other it separates out the purgation, which they call the lower belly. The kidneys are the ministries of the genital seeds, communicating with the belly and the thighs. First therefore he commands to be offered the fat which is over the belly, and the two kidneys, and the fat which is over them, that is, over the thighs, which are near the kidneys: for they are placed between the thigh and the belly.
3.4: 3.4 The caul of the liver: that is, of the liver, in which is delight or concupiscence. Hence according to the Seventy the lobe of the liver shall be taken away with the kidneys: for the liver supplies the force of operation in the kidneys.
3.6: 3.6 But if it be of the sheep, etc. ISICHIUS on Leviticus. Which ox he commands to be offered, etc., down to in the loins also is the operation of generation.
3.9: 3.9 And the tail. The Seventy: The loin without blemish, whole, lest one thing be offered to God and another to the adversary. For it is enough for this person, for pardon, not to do the things that belong to virtue; but if he works evil, he does not obtain pardon. Hence: Be ye simple as doves. For doves have exceeding simplicity, and no malice. He who offers a sacrifice from oxen has no need to offer the loin to God: for he restrains and exercises it in good works. He who immolates from goats does not have an unblemished loin to offer, because he once stained it with sin. He therefore who was not in sins can offer an unblemished loin, not he who was a sinner. For this reason in the sacrifice of peace offerings he distinguished goats from lambs.
3.17: 3.17 Neither the fat. We ought not to have our own concupiscence, that is, the carnal kind: for every man is tempted by his own concupiscence, being drawn away and allured. He forbids blood to be eaten, lest we kill anyone: for to eat blood belongs to beasts, that is, to the cruel. Therefore it is added altogether: that we may spare both our neighbors and ourselves. But the soul must be immolated to God, hence he commanded the blood to be poured out about the base of the altar.
4.1: 4.1 And the Lord spoke, etc. The soul that shall sin, etc. ORIGEN, homily 2 on Leviticus. He rightly says soul, etc., down to and the spirit a guide to virtue, if it wishes to follow him. ISICHIUS. When a soul shall sin, etc. The lawgiver omitted nothing necessary, etc., down to hence, He who knew no sin, for us was made sin.
4.3: 4.3 If the priest, etc. ORIGEN. It is to be observed that in the sin of the high priest the lawgiver does not add that he sinned ignorantly or unwillingly: for ignorance cannot befall him who was advanced to teach the rest. THE SAME. If the priest, etc. Terror and mercy together, etc., down to who is bitten by the conscience of weakness. THE SAME. If the priest, etc. The pontiff, sense of piety and religion, etc., down to is repaired by the death of Christ. An unspotted bullock to the Lord, etc. THE SAME. Secondly we find a bullock offered by the high priest as a holocaust, etc., down to in which Christ suffered.
4.5: 4.5 And he shall take also of the blood, etc. He carried the blood of the bullock into the tabernacle, that is into heaven: when after the resurrection ascending into the heavens he stood before the face of the Father, as offering the blood of the passion, interceding for us.
4.6: 4.6 Seven times: for the remission, namely, of sins and under the ministration of spiritual gifts. The blood, however, signifies the passion, according to that: I am clean from the blood of this just man. And elsewhere: His blood be upon us, etc. Of this sprinkling Peter says: Unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Christ, etc. The veil, the humanity of Christ. For as the veil was between the holy of holies and the outer tabernacle, so the flesh of Christ is between us, who are the outer tabernacle, and the divinity, which is signified by the holy of holies. Against the veil of the testimony therefore the priest sprinkled the blood of the bullock, because Christ bloodied his flesh with the blood of the passion. Against the veil, etc. He calls the flesh of the Lord by many names, because its operation is many. Hence the Lord himself named himself, now a sacrifice, Luke 21., now a shepherd, again a vine, then the bread of life and a grain of wheat, by transferred terms, John 10, 15, 6, 12. So Moses also called his flesh the veil. Hence Paul: He opened to us a way through the veil, that is his flesh, Hebrews 10. The veil also of the sanctuary is so called hence, because in it the flesh of the holy of holies is figured.
4.7: 4.7 Upon the horns. This altar signifies the seat of God, that is the Seraphim, hence Isaiah: One of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand a live coal, which he had taken with the tongs off the altar, Isaiah 6. The incense, according to the Septuagint, the compositions of all virtues. For where is it fitting that virtues be composed but in the seat of God? for from heaven they descend to us. Hence James says: But the wisdom that is from above, James 3. The four virtues, wisdom, justice, fortitude, temperance, because they contain the kinds of the other virtues, are named horns: these God anoints with his own blood, strengthening them, namely with greater and more perfect virtue, that they may prevail against adverse powers and forces. Of the altar, etc. Of angelic virtues. For if men render to God a pleasing odor of good works, how much more the holy angels remaining in purity of nature? If, however, they did not commit sin to be atoned by the blood of Christ, yet through his blood they are pacified to us, and their number repaired. At the base. The base, the lower part of the altar, signifies weak men. For by the blood of Christ not only the number of the angels was restored, but man also redeemed: therefore Christ is also called the redemption of the angels, Colossians 1. Of the altar of holocaust. Of the body of Christ. For he is priest, he sacrifice, he also altar. For as he works many things, so he is fittingly called by many names. Hence Paul: We have an altar of which they have no power to eat who serve the tabernacle, Hebrews 13.: that is the body of Christ, of which it is not lawful for the Jews to eat; this altar is at the entrance of the tabernacle, that is of heaven, because through him we have entrance to heaven. And the fat. Mystically, the delights and desires of the flesh; which yet are not all to be received in Christ, such as the desire of gluttony and coition. What he had, he had of us, as thirst and hunger, and the like. These he offered to the Father, to whose glory he transferred them, and set before us as an example, that we refer our desires to God.
4.9: 4.9 The two kidneys and the caul which is over them by the flanks. ISICHIUS. Which are done also in the sacrifice of peace offerings, or of salvation. And he divides the sacrifice in two, that the sacrifice of Christ may be lawful for all to imitate, both those, namely, who are of lower conduct, to whom the sacrifice of peace offerings is fitting, and those who follow higher things, for whom it suffices if they imitate the following.
4.11: 4.11 And the skin and all the flesh with the head and the feet and the rest. This commands that you not divide Christ, as some divide, saying: He who suffered of Mary, he who of God did not suffer; but to us there is one God Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, 1 Corinthians 8. For flesh in the Lord is all humanity, according to which it is said: The Word was made flesh, John 1. Hence he says: His flesh with the head and the feet or the extremities according to others, that by these words we may believe that he who suffered for us is the first and the last: for he is before all things, and in him all things consist. With the entrails and dung, Septuagint: with the belly and dung. The belly signifies the mind; let us not doubt therefore that he who suffered for us had a human mind, which some of the heretics deny. Dung signifies the sin of the human race, which crucified he took upon himself. Dung, though unclean, does not defile the bearer; nor is it of our nature, though it be in us: so our sins, which the Lord bore, were foreign to him, and did not defile him. The entrails and dung, etc. ORIGEN. Perhaps by comparison, etc., down to the lawgiver more fully figures his mystery in what follows.
4.13: 4.13 But if the whole multitude. ISICHIUS. He commands the same in the sacrifice of the multitude and of the priest, etc., down to for he prayed for the very crucifiers: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.
4.21: 4.21 He shall carry the bullock out of the camp. THE SAME. The conclusion of the law suffices for us to make manifest the present, for nothing is here commanded to be changed for the sin of the multitude. It is manifest that he understands the same sin of the people and of the priest, therefore in each he ordained the same sacrifice.
4.22: 4.22 If a prince shall sin and do. THE SAME. As in voluntary sacrifices, etc., down to for the sabbath was given for the rest of the wicked. ORIGEN. This prince can be called the force of reason, which is within us, which if it sins, so that we do something foolish, let us fear that sentence: You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt lose its savor, it is good for nothing but to be cast out and trodden on by men, Matthew 5.
4.23: 4.23 A he-goat of the goats. Not a she-goat, the easy namely or the middling, but a difficult and harsh penance. For the more one is eminent in understanding, the more, if he sins, for the greater fault he endures the greater penalty.
4.24: 4.24 He shall lay his hand, etc., himself making known the sin and offering his confession. He himself, according to the Septuagint, does not kill, but another; because he needs the help of others that penance may be undertaken, nor is the priest commanded to kill, for it says: And when he has immolated, etc., nor did he add who ought to immolate, for it is lawful in the sacrifice of penance to use the help of another: hence James: Pray for one another that you may be saved. Where the victim is wont to be slain, etc. Because alike pleasing to God are the worthy penance of sinners and the strong works of the just.
4.25: 4.25 The horns of the altar, etc. Upon the cross are offered the first-fruits of the blood which is offered for sin, because the work of the cross and the effect of our sins is perfect remission. And pouring out the rest. Attributing, namely, all penance to the evangelical preaching, the intent of which is that he who repents correct himself and be saved. Hence at the beginning of the Gospel the Lord providently says: Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand, Matthew 3.
4.27: 4.27 But if he sin, etc. ORIGEN, hom. 2 on Leviticus. Doing one thing from all the commandments of the Lord, etc., down to when he acknowledges to immolate the sacrifice of praise. Of the people, etc. ORIGEN. To distinguish him, etc., down to he deems necessary for our sake. But if of cattle. ISICHIUS. The offering of a she-goat which they offer who are of the people, etc., down to of she-goat and sheep he commands like things.
5.1: 5.1 If a soul sin, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 1 on Leviticus. He seems to say that a man sins, etc., down to but he immediately added: A soul that shall touch any unclean thing, etc. ISICHIUS. If he sin, etc. He does not repeat what he said above, etc., down to because we ought not to consent to another's sins or error, but rebuke.
5.2: 5.2 A soul that shall touch. ISICHIUS. Not of the body, etc., down to but he can say with David: Our soul has been delivered as a sparrow out of the snare of the fowlers, Psalm 123. GREGORY, book XXXII of Morals, ch. 4, vol. 2. To utter an oath is to bind ourselves by vow to divine servitude, etc., down to we burn with the fire of sorrow.
5.4: 5.4 The soul that shall swear, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 2 on Leviticus. What is it that for a silent perjury, or touching a carcass, or any unclean thing no sacrifice is commanded? But for the fact that one swears falsely not knowing, a lamb or a goat is decreed to be offered? or is this sacrifice to be understood for all the foregoing? For after all the things enumerated he brought in the sacrifice of expiation. And shall understand his offense. ISICHIUS. It is to be noted that offense, etc., down to as the following show.
5.7: 5.7 But if he is not able, etc. THE SAME. Let us add this, that if a prince sin in any of these, he shall offer a he-goat of the goats, a penance, namely, worthy of him, who ought neither to have sinned, nor communicated with others, nor provoked his subjects to sin. What therefore ought not to have happened, he left unexamined. But if, etc. THE SAME. He who cannot afflict himself continually, etc., down to because he most fully sacrifices himself to God.
5.8: 5.8 He shall wring the head GREGORY, hom. on Ezekiel. The death of Christ, to the conjunction of his body, etc., down to joined us all to himself more truly in his very death. GREGORY. He shall wring, etc. In the sacrifice of God we ought to be turtledoves, that our head be wrung back to the little wings, that is, the senses to the virtues. By the head we understand the mind, because as the head rules the body, so the mind the actions. But the head clings to the neck and is not cut off wholly, because our mind is to be separated from the delight of the flesh, not from the necessary care of the flesh, and let us not make provision for the flesh in its desires, Romans 13. The head of the turtledove therefore is partly cut off and partly clings to the neck. Let it be broken off, etc. He wishes us not to serve the body, but to be broken off or wrung back, lest the law of sin reign in our members. But because we ought not to hate our body, nor think it, as the heretics do, the work of the devil, but to subject it to the mind, he does not command the body to be separated from the neck, for both are the creature of one and the same.
5.9: 5.9 The foundation, etc. Septuagint, base, which is the Gospel, because according to the intention of the sacrifice of Christ and of the Gospel, a sacrifice ought to be offered for sins. Hence he adds: Because it is for sin, for nothing so rescues from sin as imitation of Christ and obedience to the evangelical preaching. But if he be not able. Because not every time is easy for penance, when namely we abuse penance itself, and destroy its fruit by returning to sin, the lawgiver hints, saying: But if his hand be not able, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 8 on Leviticus, vol. 3. It is asked whether what was said is to be taken everywhere, etc., down to that all the rest might belong from these to that generality.
5.11: 5.11 Ephah. ISICHIUS. A measure of three measures, etc., down to that those who are under his hand do not perish. He shall not put on it, etc. As if: this is not perfect penance, therefore it has no oil, that is spiritual joy of cheerfulness, nor frankincense, because he is not to be confident in prayers: but let him who offers the oblation deliver it to the priest, that is entrust the hope of salvation to the divine mercy. Who for sin. Because he knows not whether the prayer of one who frequently transgresses is of good odor. Hence: Who knows if God will turn and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him? John 3. He does not allow therefore to despair, nor yet to presume, lest they again be negligent.
5.12: 5.12 A handful. In the handful Scripture is signified, with which it is written. It is written, however: I say not to you till seven times, but till seventy times seven times, Matthew 28. By the handful therefore he hints that God is to be entreated to remember his written mercy, that he may give it to us: as he commands it to be given to brethren; for this the great priest will cleanse the one praying.
5.13: 5.13 A soul if transgressing, etc. ISICHIUS. One must abstain from every sin, but most from that which is committed against holy things: how dreadful it is the offering attests. For nowhere from the beginning of the history, except in this place, is a ram commanded to be offered, in which the necessity and utility of the sacrifice are declared: here is offered neither he-goat, nor she-goat, nor sheep, nor a pair of turtledoves, nor two young pigeons. Ceremonies by, etc. ORIGEN. There are many kinds of sanctification. There is the oil with which the tabernacle alone is anointed; and the incense, of which it is said: Whoever shall make the like composition shall perish from among his people: the loaves of proposition also only males eat, who are of the stock of Aaron. Mystically, however, in the things that are sanctified he sins who in a sacred place irreverently usurps anything or handles divine things unworthily.
5.15: 5.15 Two shekels. The two shekels are the two precepts of charity, with which the sinner buys for himself confidence of remission. For penance is worth nothing without the grace of remission; hence according to the Septuagint the ram is bought with fifty shekels, because through penance and the observance of twofold charity perfect rest is acquired, when remission of sins is given. Septuagint, fifty shekels of silver, shekel of the sanctuary. For no one acquires the sacrifice of the Lord except through the Holy Spirit, because no one can say Lord Jesus but in the Holy Spirit, 1 Corinthians 12. Fifty signifies the coming of the Holy Spirit, because on the day of Pentecost, that is the fiftieth, he came to the apostles. Septuagint: shekel of the sanctuary. In the shekel of the sanctuary he signified the virtue and operation of the Holy Spirit. The shekel is of 20 obols, the twenty-year-old is not liable to sin: hence those who went out of Egypt when they were twenty years old did not undergo the punishment of the sin of the people, Numbers 14.; the spiritual man is clean from every sin.
5.16: 5.16 And the fifth part, etc. ISICHIUS. He who with a holy vessel or food, etc., down to for so he will make supplication for our sin.
5.17: 5.17 A soul if he sin, etc. THE SAME. He seems to have forgotten what he had commanded: for the sins for which he commanded a she-goat or sheep to be offered, now he seems to command a ram to be offered; but he neither forgot the former nor commanded contrary things: for there by soul he signified the Gentile: here he signifies him who transgresses the commands of the law through ignorance. AUGUSTINE, question 7 on Leviticus. It is asked how this offense is distinguished from those which he has generally embraced, etc., down to or some in sacred services.
5.18: 5.18 He shall offer a ram, etc. Above he commanded the penitent to offer a she-goat, here he commands a ram to be immolated, because it profits nothing to immolate the harshness of penance unless you have resolved to have full confidence in the immolation of Christ.
6.1: 6.1 He spoke, etc. The soul that sins, etc. ISICHIUS. It is the same sin as in holy things, etc., down to it is like robbery. ORIGEN, hom. 4 on Leviticus. The soul that sins, etc. I think that our soul, etc., down to For no man puts new wine into old bottles. A thing lost, etc. ORIGEN. Septuagint: destruction. The heretics labor to find destruction in the Scriptures, whence they can build error: but perhaps hearing ecclesiastical words they come to themselves, and what they had found they understand to be destruction and render it back, that is give it up to its author.
6.5: 6.5 And the fifth part besides, etc. The tongue, namely, in which is one of the five senses: this is offered that henceforth he not sin, because through it each of the aforesaid was committed. ORIGEN. Septuagint: not the fifth part but fifths, as twice five, etc., down to we refer to one God.
6.8: 6.8 And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying. ISICHIUS. Here he speaks of the perpetual sacrifice, etc., down to and compose his whole life to perfection.
6.10: 6.10 Linen, not woolen, the tunic and breeches he wills to be linen, not woolen, Exodus 28. For the linen garment is handy and soft and clinging to the body; woolen is rough, because justice and chastity are handy and much clinging to the soul. A linen garment also can easily be had, so also virtues, if one wishes to obtain them. And he shall take up the ashes, etc. Ash is the consummation of good work. Aaron shall carry the ashes outside the camp, who after this life present good works to God the Father through Christ the great pontiff. And there they are reduced to ashes while he stands before the face of God for us. For the camp is the present life, in which we ever fight against spiritual wickedness, Hebrews 9. They are put beside the altar, while the consummation of good works is laid up in the ark of the heart. For the altar in this place signifies the heart. This is our glory, the testimony of conscience, etc., Ephesians last.
6.11: 6.11 And clothed with other. ORIGEN. It is to be observed that the priest uses other garments in the mystery of the sacrifices, and others when he goes forth to the people. Hence: We speak wisdom among the perfect, 1 Corinthians 1. And elsewhere, clothed in a far lower robe, he says: I judged not myself to know anything among you but Jesus Christ, and him crucified, 1 Corinthians 1.
6.12: 6.12 The fire on. AUGUSTINE, question 12 on Leviticus. He does not wish the fire to be altogether put out, but when the holocaust has burned till morning, the remains being removed it is renewed again, that other things that are laid on may burn. Which the priest shall feed. Allegorically. In the morning Christ was judged, in the evening crucified. The fire therefore is fed morning and evening: because the charity of God is nourished in us while we recall Christ judged in the morning, crucified in the evening. GREGORY, book XXV of Morals, ch. 7. The altar of God is our heart, etc., down to that the more God is seen the more he is loved. And the holocaust being laid on it, he shall burn upon it, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 13 on Leviticus. It is to be seen whether any day was left out, etc., down to which it would be wonderful if he were silent, nor admonished that such things be offered in the evening.
6.14: 6.14 This is. The lawgiver seems to repeat what he has said, renewing the memory by repetition of the commandment and showing the usefulness and necessity of the law. Yet he interposes something new by which he hints the commandment is necessary and inexcusable. As therefore concerning holocausts he repeated the sacrifices, mingling with them constancy, as is that: The fire on the altar shall always burn and never go out: so in the sacrifice of fine flour, that is of theology, he adds that it must be eaten only in a holy place and by a male. And before. According as Christ, who is the true altar, shall reveal. In these therefore let us establish theology which the incarnate Christ has delivered to us, that we may think the Father in him and him in the Father, and that he is the Spirit of the Son and proceeds from the Father.
6.16: 6.16 The rest, etc., that we may not wholly cease from theology, because the sum of knowledge is concerned with the future. In the place. The Church, which is the entrance and vestibule of heaven, in it it is fitting to speak of the Divinity, hence Psalm 67: In the churches bless God, each one is a domestic church to himself, when he ceases from earthly business: here he can speak to himself of God and exercise theology. Such are they to whom part of the sacrifice is given, to meditate, namely, and speak of God.
6.17: 6.17 As for sin. He hints this sacrifice is like that which is both for sin and for offense: for the discourse about God is held chiefly for expiation and cleansing of the soul, when to oil and frankincense, that is to alms and prayer, the sacrifice of the word of God, that is of theology, is joined.
6.18: 6.18 Only the males. It is not for everyone to dispute of God, but for those who have nothing womanish, nothing fluid in thoughts or works. It is a lawful and everlasting ordinance. For we ought not to presume to dispute of God while through secular fancies we decline from the dignity of males. Everyone that shall touch. ISICHIUS. This cannot stand according to the letter: for will a murderer or a profane person be sanctified if he touch? for no one is excepted. But Christ, in whose type these things went before, is immolated: whoever touches his flesh, that is, who with faithful heart has placed all hope of salvation in his passion and resurrection, shall be sanctified forthwith. THE SAME. Everyone who, etc. Every remembrance of God affords sanctification. Hence: It is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. But when he says that the one touching is sanctified, he plainly shows that in disputing of God, that is in doing theology, it suffices us only to touch: for he who wishes to be warmed, if he puts his hand into the fire, will suffer burning instead of warming. This is the oblation. AUGUSTINE, question 14 on Leviticus. There are other sacrifices which he mentioned in Exodus, by which for seven days the priests are sanctified, that they may perform the priesthood. It is another that he mentions, which the high priest offers when he is appointed, that is when he is anointed: hence he adds: In the day that he shall anoint him, not them, though he commands also the second priests to be anointed; this sacrifice is everlasting by succession, namely of the priests. Or because what it signifies is everlasting. This is, etc. Aaron, mountain of strength, that is Christ; his sons all the faithful; the day of anointing, the time of the incarnation, when he was anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows. The ephah. The humanity of Christ. The ephah, containing three measures, signifies the Trinity, if indeed the ephah is the flesh of the Lord, that the eminence of divinity and the inseparability of the Lord's flesh with it may be shown, yet the sacrifice is perpetual. For by one oblation he has perfected forever those who are sanctified: hence he can also save forever. In the sacrifice. ORIGEN. The law of Moses is the sacrifice of the priest, etc., down to in which nothing is remiss, nothing luxurious, Matthew 16. Morning. In the morning the passion of the Lord began from when in the court of Caiaphas he was struck with blows, and it was prolonged till evening, for darkness interrupting it from the sixth hour to the ninth hour it is divided into morning and evening.
6.21: 6.21 Which in the frying-pan. GREGORY, hom. 12 on Ezekiel. No such sacrifice is God's, etc., down to the holocaust is deputed to God.
6.22: 6.22 The priest. Septuagint: The anointed priest of his sons in his place shall do these things. For Christ is in place of Aaron, not in his seat, because he transferred the priesthood to himself and took Aaron away. Of his sons, because he descended from Jacob through Mary and of the same tribe. Who to the Father. One Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, Romans 11. For the Lord of glory was crucified, and the passion of the incarnate Word is that which was in the flesh of Christ: Who emptied himself wholly, taking the form of a servant and obedient to the Father unto death on the cross.
6.23: 6.23 For every. Whatever in the sacrifice of peace offerings he commands to be done, in this also. Nor shall any. What is eaten is broken: he breaks the sacrifice of Christ who says he died for sins when he committed no sin. ORIGEN. Nor shall any eat. The sacrifice in this place is to be taken as the Word itself, and doctrine, of which no one eats, that is disputes or retracts; but it is holocaust. For whatever he said, whatever he established, endures in eternal consecration. The priest who, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 18 on Leviticus. Not what he lays on, etc., down to this he briefly mentions now. ORIGEN, hom. 5 on Leviticus. Some of the victims are God's alone, etc., down to better we reserve these for the fire.
6.27: 6.27 Whatsoever shall touch. Although the offering be another's, that is the penitent's, it shall be sanctified though he do not repent. Similarly if a little child be baptized, who of himself has not yet sinned, he is cleansed from the original If of the blood, that is if the substance of the flesh has been stained by sins. Hence: The garment mixed with blood shall be in the burning, and fuel of fire, Isaiah 9. of hell, namely shall be washed in a holy place, that is it shall have hope in baptism, which not only washes the past but instructs that one may repent of the future.
6.28: 6.28 But the earthen vessel, etc. The weak: the feeble, namely, who, penance completed, relapses into sins, these are to be broken by the terror of judgment.
6.29: 6.29 Every male, etc. The priest offering and eating the whole sacrifice is Christ, who offers our penance, and eats the salvation of sinners. The flesh of the sacrifice, however, because they pertain to penance, every male of the priests eats, the strong, namely, and vigorous, to whom it is said: Do manfully, and let your heart take courage, and wait for the Lord, Psalm 26.
6.30: 6.30 It shall not be eaten, etc. Because it pertains to Christ, who by his own authority and by the power of his own divinity grants remission. For his passion, by which remission is procured for us, was not of a mere man but of God incarnate. Therefore it is not eaten by men, but is consumed by fire, because to give remission is of God alone, who is signified by fire, for our God is a consuming fire, Deuteronomy 4.
7.1: 7.1 Offense. ISICHIUS. Offense he sometimes says, etc., down to but the offering of the kidneys and the lobe of the liver and thighs is holiness. ORIGEN, question 5 on Leviticus. Some say there is offense when we do not do what we ought: sin when we do what we ought not, but this is not observed everywhere.
7.2: 7.2 The blood thereof, etc. ISICHIUS. Whatever is done in the sacrifice of peace offerings he commands to be done in this also.
7.7: 7.7 As for sin, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 20 on Leviticus. Sin is the perpetration of evil, offense the desertion of good. For as it is one thing to decline from evil and another to do good, so it is one thing to abstain from good and another to do evil, and that be offense, this sin. Or offense is what is committed ignorantly, sin what knowingly. ORIGEN, as above. As for sin, etc. Likewise the fat of the ram is commanded, etc., down to that is, that they convert the sinner from the way of sin. To the priest, etc. Christ, who for us was made propitiation. In him therefore every sacrifice is ministered and done, and what is gained by penance is referred to him. For he, to save us, came saying: I came not to call the just, but sinners, Matthew 9. The victim of the holocaust. ISICHIUS. Not good, namely, or of sheep, etc., down to in respect of whom we have patience in sufferings.
7.9: 7.9 He shall have the skin. The circumstance of riches, which they ought to offer to the true priest who wish a holocaust to be made. Satan named the circumstance of riches a skin, saying: Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life, Job 2. This Job gave as a skin, that is that he retain patience, which is called skin from which many useful things are made. And whatever on the gridiron, etc. Because these are next to the theology of the incarnation, they necessarily belong to the offering priest, that is Christ born, suffered, and risen.
7.10: 7.10 Whether sprinkled with oil, etc. ORIGEN, hom. 5 on Leviticus. The sacrifice is commanded to be made in oil, etc., down to another in the frying-pan, the third on the gridiron. ISICHIUS. The sacrifice sprinkled with oil he says of fine flour, etc., down to he assigned to the sons of Aaron.
7.12: 7.12 If the oblation be for thanksgiving. According to the letter the oblation for thanksgiving is made when one, delivered from great tribulation, gives thanks, as Moses after the passage of the Red Sea, Exodus 15. Mystically also, he who has not committed greater crimes pays the praises of God's mercy, who has kept himself free from horrible crimes. And unleavened cakes anointed with oil. Bread, namely, thin and broad, which signifies the knowledge of the prophets. As great as is the distance between the solidity of bread and the tenderness of the cake, so great is that between the knowledge of the Old and New Testament; the loaves therefore are sprinkled with oil, the cakes anointed, because the light and grace of the New Testament is greater than that of the Old. And fine flour fried, and cakes of oil, etc. The divine wisdom, namely, which is cooked by the fire of charity. For Christ, the wisdom of God, for exceeding charity delivers himself to death.
7.14: 7.14 It shall be offered to the Lord, and shall be the priest's, etc. Septuagint: And he shall offer of all his gifts the praise of God to the priest pouring out the blood, and it shall be his of salvation. For it is not of him that wills nor of him that runs, but of God that shows mercy, Romans 9. To Christ ministering and perfecting the sacrifice the first-fruits are to be offered.
7.15: 7.15 The flesh of which shall be eaten the same day, etc. ORIGEN, as above. One food of the soul is of milk, etc., down to Let them be, he says, new and old. Until morning. The future age, where there will be the true day which succeeds the night of this age, does not will our imperfect life to be left through which it behooves us to be saved: for in the future it will not be lawful to work.
7.16: 7.16 If by vow or voluntarily, etc. Every sacrifice of peace offerings or of salvation is voluntary, hence it is placed among gifts above. But the sacrifice of thanksgiving or praise, although it be a species of it, because it is reasonable, is not called voluntary: because, since we are rational, we owe in a way a special debt to the Creator, a reasonable sacrifice. The same likewise. Because some after the end of this life have described another like it, introducing a certain age of a thousand years in which Jerusalem is built and its temple, and the holy of holies are restored, and sacrifices offered. But if anyone believes this and in a way eats it in mind, hoping to eat at that time, which is impossible, his offering is not received, because polluted, and he contracts sin also, hence he says: Whatever soul shall have defiled itself with such food, etc. But if any, etc. ORIGEN, as above. The two days on which it is lawful to eat the flesh of the sacrifice, etc., down to let us not therefore assume the knowledge of all.
7.17: 7.17 On the third day. The future age in which is the general resurrection, which the resurrection of Christ signified. The morning of the third day having come, then what remains shall be consumed with fire: whatever saving thing we have left imperfect, or evil we have done, like wood, hay, or stubble, shall be consumed with fire: but we shall suffer loss, 1 Corinthians 3.
7.19: 7.19 The flesh which, etc. ORIGEN, hom. 5 on Leviticus. The holy flesh is understood as divine words, etc., down to and is polluted by foreign uncleanness.
7.21: 7.21 Or of a beast. The beasts are unclean who are intent on unclean and earthly actions, hence fornicators are called stud horses.
7.23: 7.23 The fat of the sheep, etc. That is neither of the strong, nor of the innocent, nor of the penitent, is the good intention or desire to be depraved by an evil interpretation as if it were done through hypocrisy, lest anyone wish to destroy another's merit, and as if by eating diminish it. AUGUSTINE, question 21 on Leviticus, vol. 3. He said above, etc., down to they chose for themselves the death of sin.
7.24: 7.24 To various uses. Not only by imitating the works of the good, but also by drawing the wicked to us as an example. For we read that Herod celebrated his birthday and stained the feasts with blood, Matthew 14.: such a desire we have for use that we may beware, but on the contrary may recall the day of our birth on which we were in paradise, with mourning and affliction. The proud Pharisee says: I thank you that I am not as the rest of men, etc., Luke 18. Let us on the contrary say: God, have mercy on me, for I am not like your servants, who lead an angelic life on earth.
7.25: 7.25 If any man eat the fat, etc. ORIGEN. As if: let no one scandalize one of these little ones who believe in me, etc. Blood is forbidden to be eaten, as if, glory not against the broken branches, lest you be cut off, and they, if they continue not in unbelief, be grafted in, Romans 11. Blood, however, is rightly understood as the people of the Jews: for it descended not from the faith nor from the spirit of Abraham, but only from his blood.
7.29: 7.29 He that offers the victim. ORIGEN, hom. 5 on Leviticus. Another reading, etc., down to and conscious of his salvation gives thanks to the Lord. THE SAME, ibid. The sacrifice which is called salutary, etc., down to who carry the vessels of the Lord.
7.30: 7.30 He shall hold in his hands, etc. JEROME, letter to Fabiola, vol. 1. From the salutary victims the priests offer the fat, etc., down to that he may learn to despise what he sees cast into the privy. Septuagint: Offering a salutary sacrifice to the Lord, he shall offer his gift to the Lord from his salutary sacrifice. Which expounding he adds: He shall hold in his hands the fat of the victim. Or according to the Septuagint: his hands shall offer from it to the Lord: For it behooves him to work what pertains to his own salvation: for the justice of the just shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him, Ezekiel 18. And the breast shall be, etc. ISIDORE. The breast is given to the priest that he may have clean thought and knowledge of doctrine. The right arm, that he may have good works, and go forth to the battle against the devil with armed hand, and perfect by example of works what he has conceived in heart. The jaw too is given from the private, that he may excel in eloquence: the belly is given, that he may extinguish luxury and despise gluttony.
7.32: 7.32 Of the priest. AUGUSTINE. Of Christ, figured in the priest. Hence the priest alone can perfect this sacrifice. For to begin the good is ours: to perfect and bring to the end is of divine grace. It is not of him that wills nor of him that runs, but of God that shows mercy to direct the actions: hence it is also called the arm of God. Hence rightly he received the shoulder or, according to the Septuagint: the arm.
7.33: 7.33 He that shall offer the blood, etc. It is Christ, who offers the true blood of the peace offerings and the fat, the souls namely and the desires of the saved, who is of the sons of Aaron the priest singular and in all things chief, to whom falls the right shoulder as his portion, that is, every good and perfect action.
7.35: 7.35 This is the anointing. ISICHIUS. These things seem therefore to pertain to the anointing of the priests, etc., down to what he understood by the aforesaid anointing he shows in what follows.
7.37: 7.37 This is the law of the holocaust, etc. ORIGEN, hom. 5. When the lawgiver has proposed, etc., down to in which the truth of the figures is preserved. This is the law, etc. ISICHIUS. You see the different ways of life that join to God, namely honor, the perfect of wisdom, which is signified by the holocaust; or the middling justice, which does the things that are for salvation. For the law understood that the sacrifices of peace offerings are rightly useful to the priestly dignity either through the holocaust or through the oblation. Hence in the day in which he commanded the law of anointing he added what concerns the sacrifices and at once briefly mentioned all.
7.38: 7.38 In Mount Sinai. Which is interpreted bush or temptation: temptation is like a bush: for it is a rough shrub and is hard to grasp: so the crown of a good life in temptations and tribulations is scarcely had. Hence: Blessed is the man that endures temptation, for when he has been proved he shall receive the crown of life, James 2.
8.2: 8.2 Two rams. The passion of Christ, who is the leader of the people, is signified. Well are two rams immolated, because Christ twice committed to us the mysteries of his passion: first when he ate the mystic lamb at the supper, second when he established the same mysteries in the consecration of bread and wine.
8.3: 8.3 And you shall gather. Moses called together all the synagogue, although the Lord had chosen and commanded, yet the synagogue is called together: for in ordaining a priest the presence of the people is required, that all may know and be sure that the one who is more excellent of all the people, more learned, holier and more eminent in virtue, is chosen to the priesthood. He washed him therefore and clothed him. With what garment? the tunic, and girded him with the girdle. And again: He clothed him with a tunic to the ankles, Ecclesiasticus 45., or, as we read elsewhere, an inner one, 2 Kings 15. I see the high priest clothed with two tunics. But Jesus forbids the apostles to be clothed with two tunics, since Moses and Jesus, that is the law and the Gospel, ought to agree, Matthew 10. Others say that Jesus commanded not to have two tunics, which is not contrary to the law but more perfect than the law: as also when the law forbids murder, Exodus 20., Jesus cuts off anger, Matthew 5.; and when the law forbids adultery, Jesus cuts off concupiscence. I do not shut up the pontifical sacraments within the narrowness of this understanding: something more seems to me shown from this form. That high priest whom Moses was then ordaining knew that circumcision was spiritual: yet he kept also the circumcision of the flesh, because he could not be uncircumcised, he had therefore two tunics, one of the carnal mystery, another of spiritual understanding. For he could not be high priest of those who then were unless he offered carnal sacrifices, although he knew they ought to be spiritual. Fittingly therefore he had two tunics. But the apostles who were going to say: If you be circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing, Galatians 5., and were utterly to reprobate the literal observance, are rightly forbidden to have two tunics; one suffices them, and this the inner one, but the outer tunic of the law they do not want, because Jesus permits them to have one and that the inner one.
8.6: 8.6 And when he had washed. JEROME as above. Already then the purgation of the world, etc., down to that what we conceive in mind we may perpetrate in work. ORIGEN, hom. 6 on Leviticus. Let Moses wash you, etc., down to in what order the high priest is constituted.
8.7: 8.7 He clothed. JEROME, ibid. Let us first learn the common vestments of the priests, etc., down to because in a web such a work cannot be done. THE SAME. The second is of linen, the poderes, that is the ankle-length, of double linen, which Josephus calls byssine; this adheres to the body so close and with tight sleeves that there is no wrinkle in the garment, and it descends to the legs. Soldiers are wont to have such linen ones, which they call shirts, fitting the limbs and tight, that they may be ready for everything. This tunic the priests use, having the beauty of the clothed and the speed of the naked, which is called linen. The third the girdle, most like the skin of a serpent which it casts off in summer, a long purse woven round, under a covering of scarlet, purple, hyacinth and byssus: for beauty and strength, so variegated that you would think the various flowers and gems not woven but added by the craftsman's hand. With this belt between the navel and breast the linen tunic is bound, which, having the breadth of four fingers and descending for the most part to the legs, when there is need for sacrifices is thrown back over the left shoulder. JEROME. The fourth is round, etc., down to about to die at once. THE SAME. The sixth in Hebrew, etc., down to he may carry on his shoulders. THE SAME. The seventh is small, etc., down to and by one weave seemed to the beholders. THE SAME. The eighth is the golden plate, etc., down to and the name of God crown and protect the whole beauty of the high priest. The pomegranates and the bells placed on the lower parts show lightnings and thunders, or earth and water and all the elements harmonizing with each other, and so interwoven that in each are all. JEROME. The Hebrews four colors, etc., down to providence penetrates all things. ORIGEN, hom. 6 on Leviticus. In Exodus, where it is commanded about priestly garments, etc., down to lest the holy be given to dogs and pearls be cast before swine, Mark 7. And putting on, etc. Septuagint: He put on the tunic and girded him with the girdle and clothed him with the ephod. He follows out the incarnation of Christ. For he took the whole man, body namely and soul; the tunic he called earthly, because it is of earth; the ephod heavenly, because it is from the poderes. And the hyacinth, which is a heavenly color: for he took both, and saved both. JEROME. In the hyacinth tunic, pomegranates, and bells: because so great ought to be the knowledge of the high priest that his step and motion and all be vocal, and the truth which he conceived in mind resound in his bearing; whatever he does, whatever he says, be doctrine. Without bells, diverse colors, gems, and flowers of virtues neither does he enter the Church, nor is he high priest. The ephod, etc. ORIGEN. Moses put on the high priest the superhumeral, which is the adornment of the garment drawn round the shoulders: the shoulders are signs of labor and work. He wills therefore the high priest to be adorned in works: for knowledge alone does not suffice, but he who shall do and teach, he shall be called great, 1 Timothy 3; Matthew 5. The superhumeral. JEROME. The superhumeral and the two emerald or onyx stones which cover the shoulders above are interpreted the two hemispheres, one above the earth, the other under the earth; or the sun and moon that glow above. THE SAME. The two stones in the superhumeral Christ and the Church, containing the names of the twelve apostles who were sent to preach, or the letter and the spirit in which are all the mysteries of the law; on the right the spirit, on the left the letter, 2 Corinthians 3. Through letters we come to words, through words to the sense. A beautiful order signifying the sacraments by the very habit: on the shoulders works, on the breast reason, hence the priests also eat the breast.
8.8: 8.8 Which binding. ORIGEN, as above. He girded him according to the making of the ephod, etc., down to because according to his works he uses the girdle of virtue. He fitted the rational, etc. JEROME. The rational placed in the middle indicates the earth, which like a point, though having all things in itself, is surrounded by all the elements. ORIGEN, as above. He put on him the logion, etc., down to for nothing is added after this to the head of the high priest. JEROME, as above. The rational double, open and hidden, etc., down to and these going before, doctrine and truth follow. THE SAME. The twelve stones, etc., down to knowledge being shown to us. He put the plate. THE SAME. The learning of all profits nothing unless crowned with the knowledge of God, which is ever with him and the Father: hence he put the plate upon the cidaris. THE SAME. All things are imperfect unless a charioteer is sought for the chariot and the Creator standing over creatures himself rules who made them. What formerly in the plate, now is shown in the sign of the cross: the blood of the Gospel is more precious than the gold of the law; then according to Ezekiel the sign Tau was fixed on the foreheads of the groaning, Ezekiel 8.: now bearing the cross we say: The light of your countenance is signed upon us, O Lord, etc., Psalm 4. The golden plate on the forehead of the high priest, and the name of God inscribed, signifies that all things on earth are governed by the will of God. For it was just that the high priest of God, bearing the type of all creatures in his vestments, should indicate that all need the mercy of God, and when he sacrificed, the universal condition was expiated: where not for children, parents and kin, but for all creation by voice and bearing he prayed.
8.10: 8.10 He took, etc. It is the Son of God himself, who anoints and who is anointed: anointing by the word of divinity, according to which he has all things common with the Father and the Holy Spirit. He is anointed by the Father according to that: God, your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness, etc., Psalm 44. The Holy Spirit anointed him according to Isaiah: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me, Isaiah 61. What the Father and the Holy Spirit do, the Son also does. He anoints therefore according to divinity, is anointed according to humanity. Hence Daniel also sees him offered, does not see him offering, because he offers himself. Moses therefore anoints and offers, bearing the figure of Christ.
8.11: 8.11 They sanctify. ORIGEN. It signifies the higher creature enriched by our sanctification: that is, through the Lord's flesh taken from us. Hence: that it might be made known to the principalities and powers through the church, etc.
8.12: 8.12 Pouring, etc. The head of Christ is the divinity. For as the head is not divided from the feet, so neither is the divinity of Christ from the humanity after the anointing, 1 Corinthians 11. Hence he says: God has anointed you, O God your God, etc., Psalm 54. So God is anointed and sanctified.
8.13: 8.13 The sons, etc. ORIGEN, as above. Attend to the difference of the lesser priests to the greater, etc., down to even if the first has received the name. And he clothed, etc. To the sons of Aaron like tunics and girdles or belts and cidaris or miters are put on, for they put him on, are girded with him, bear him on the head; for the loins are girded with truth, which is Christ, and clothed with the breastplate of justice: Christ however is justice, as also the helmet of salvation, for he is the salvation of God.
8.14: 8.14 He offered, etc. ISICHIUS. What the power of this law is, etc., down to necessarily the sons of Aaron as sharing in the sacrifice lay on hands. AUGUSTINE, question 23 on Leviticus. When he recalled the sacrifices for sins, etc., down to and the blood poured out at the base of the altar of the sacrifices. He offered, etc. ISICHIUS. The law, the priest figuring Christ in many things, etc., down to commanded for sheep. He offered, etc. The tradition of the mysteries, and the mystic Passover, which Christ celebrated with his disciples, Matthew 26., the ram signifies: it is named second, because after the lamb immolated at the supper he offered himself; hence Aaron laid hands on the head of the ram with his sons, because Christ celebrated the common supper with his disciples; but Moses offered this sacrifice specially, because he expressed the figure of Christ more than the others, who most made his sacrifice.
8.24: 8.24 He touched the tip of the ear, etc. If by Aaron we understand Christ, the tip of his ear was touched with blood, because he obeyed the Father even unto death. If the priests of the Church, their ears are to be touched, and the thumbs of hands and feet, that they consecrate to the Lord the eminence of their actions and steps. He touched the tip, etc. What is the effect of this sacrifice the anointing of ears and hands and feet shows: for our obedience and good actions and conduct it is celebrated, that, lacking the disobedience of Adam, we may obtain the obedience of the Only-begotten. His hands, etc. That we be strengthened in good action. For those which are anointed are strengthened, those which are not anointed are destroyed. For where there was no anointing of the immolated blood, Egypt was struck. But first the priest and afterward his sons were anointed with blood, because Christ first took the blood at the supper, then gave it to the disciples. He poured it upon the altar. For when he drank and gave the apostles to drink, he poured the intelligible blood upon the altar, that is his body. The Church however is the body of Christ; hence Mark: And taking, giving thanks, he gave to them, and they all drank of it, and he said to them: This is my blood of the new testament, which shall be shed for many, Mark 14. But the fat. What these signify, in the salutary sacrifice, or of peace offerings, has been said. The Septuagint for tail, loin; for entrails, stomach; and for the caul of the liver, lobe of the liver: not in vain are they commemorated even now in the ram.
8.26: 8.26 In the basket. Septuagint, the basket: of consummation, which is the tongue of the Lord, which introduced the chief and perfect doctrine. For he came not to destroy the law, but to fulfill it, Matthew 13. This is well called a basket because of the weaving of his doctrine, since he had spoken many things in parables. It was also the dish and table of all doctrine. Rightly therefore from the basket of consummation he sets forth the mystic bread. Bread. The apostolic doctrine, and legal, and prophetic. For the law, and the prophets, and the apostles make memory of him. The law says: This is the bread which the Lord has given you, Exodus 26. The prophet: His bread shall be given, etc., Isaiah 33. Prophetic and legal doctrine nourish less than apostolic. Hence Paul: God has set in the church first apostles, secondly prophets, 1 Corinthians 12. The apostles bring the testimonies of the law and the prophets, by which the cakes and wafers are placed under them. And the shoulder. GREGORY, book 1 of Register, letter 24.
